items.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006
items.q: Dick Sherman will give you the history of jazz up to that point... We were the three Hamilton guys... Dick Sherman has got me listening to George Brunies

ctx.x: Now what’s the history — do you know about the history of the name the Catatonic Five?

I really don’t. And I bet you Donny Andre can tell you about that. And Dick Sherman will give you the history of jazz up to that point. But this was fall of ’55. And the band that came together was Em Brown, who was a senior, he was the clarinetist and the leader, Donny Andre was a sophomore and the banjo player and became the manager of the band and really did a yeoman job getting the gigs and doing all the hard work of running a band, and myself, a brand new trombonist just trying to learn how to play the…
And from a very musical family too, with Tori who went on with Tony Bennett and all that.

items.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006
items.q: And Phil Mead, his trombone slide hits the hat.

ctx.x: I’ve always insisted that the straw hats be worn. And it’s been, I think a boon to us because our publicity is very good. The pictures of us in the Alumni Review for example with the hats on are terrific, it’s a uniform thing. But lately I’m getting a lot of resistance to wearing the hats. And two sources. Gordy Bourns says, “When I wear the hat I can’t play the tuba, the tuba hits it.” And Phil Mead, his trombone slide hits the hat. And that is absolutely right, those are justifiable complaints.
